title: Carbon cycle

definition.text: The part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere.

facts.text: Carbon is the main component of biological compounds and also a major part of many rocks, such as limestone.
The cycle is usually divided into reservoirs, or carbon pools: the atmosphere, the terrestrial biosphere (including soils), the ocean, sediments and Earth's interior.
Carbon passes between these pools through chemical, physical, geological and biological processes; the ocean holds the largest active pool near Earth's surface.
Photosynthesis is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the atmosphere and enters land and ocean life.
Without human influence the natural flows between atmosphere, ocean, land ecosystems and sediments are fairly balanced, so carbon levels would stay roughly stable.
Humans have disturbed the cycle for centuries by changing land use and by mining and burning coal, petroleum and gas.
By 2020 atmospheric carbon dioxide had risen nearly 52% above pre-industrial levels, causing global warming.
Land and ocean sinks each currently take up about one-quarter of human carbon emissions every year.

definition.text: The split of the carbon cycle into a fast biological cycle that turns over in years and a slow geological cycle that takes millions of years.

facts.text: The fast cycle runs through living things, moving carbon between the atmosphere, land and marine ecosystems, soils and seafloor sediments.
It includes annual cycles driven by photosynthesis and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition.
The slow cycle runs through rocks: weathering returns carbon to the atmosphere by degassing and to the ocean by rivers, over spans of millions of years.
Between 10 and 100 million tonnes of carbon move around the slow cycle in a given year.

title: Terrestrial carbon pool

definition.text: The carbon held on land, in all living and dead land organisms and in soils.

facts.text: About 500 gigatons of carbon are stored above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds approximately 1,500 gigatons.
Most land carbon is organic, but about a third of soil carbon is held in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate.
Because land uptake depends on living things, it follows daily and seasonal cycles that show up in the Keeling curve of CO2 measurements.
Carbon leaves the land pool by burning or respiration, by export to the ocean in rivers, or stays sequestered in soils as inert carbon.
Soil carbon can stay put for up to thousands of years before erosion washes it into rivers or soil respiration releases it.
How long soil holds carbon depends on local climate, so it changes as the climate changes.
Forests hold 86% of the planet's land above-ground carbon, and forest soils hold 73% of its soil carbon.
About half of gross primary production is respired straight back by plants; of the rest, part goes to fires and heterotrophic respiration and part becomes slower-cycling soil organic carbon.

definition.text: The release of land carbon to the atmosphere when people clear or convert vegetation, chiefly by turning forest into farmland or towns.

facts.text: Since the invention of agriculture, people have shifted the carbon cycle over centuries by changing the mix of vegetation on land.
Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon, so replacing forest with them leaves more carbon in the atmosphere.
Land-use change has also cut biodiversity, lowering ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air.
The effect can be reversed, deliberately or naturally, by reforestation.

title: Soil carbon

definition.text: The solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from plants, animals and microbes and as inorganic carbonate minerals.

facts.text: Soil carbon underpins water holding capacity, nutrient retention and soil structure.
Soils hold about 2,700 Gt of carbon, 1550 GtC organic and 950 GtC inorganic, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere.
Peat and wetlands hold a further 150 GtC and surface plant litter 50 GtC.
Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes setting how much carbon is stored on land.
About 60 GtC a year accumulates in soil, and an equivalent 60 GtC a year is respired from soil back to the atmosphere.
As a carbon sink in the global cycle, soil carbon matters for climate change mitigation, and data on it feed global climate models.
Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil organic carbon, but people could also deliberately return carbon to the soil.
Global data on soil organic carbon are inconsistent, with some regions far better covered than others.

title: Soil inorganic carbon

definition.text: Carbon held in soil as minerals, mainly carbonates, formed by weathering of parent material or by soil minerals reacting with atmospheric CO2.

facts.text: In arid and semi-arid environments most soil carbon is inorganic, as carbonates such as calcite and dolomite.
Carbonates can come from the bedrock or parent material, or form in place in the soil as pedogenic carbonate.
Inorganic carbon makes up about 950 GtC of the world's soil carbon, roughly a third of the total.
The reactions are reversible: when carbonate meets hydrogen ions from acids, as in soils, it forms water and releases CO2 back to the air.

title: Soil organic carbon

definition.text: The carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight.

facts.text: In humid environments most soil carbon is organic.
Its main source is dead plant material added as roots, fallen leaves and crop residue; animal bodies and excreta add more.
Plants supply 5–20% of the carbon they fix by photosynthesis to the soil as root exudates feeding rhizosphere organisms such as mycorrhizal fungi.
Cellulose, starches, proteins and lipids break down fast, while lignin, humus, aggregate-bound organic matter and charcoal resist change and persist long.
Microbes cycle soil carbon so thoroughly that their dead remains, microbial necromass, can make up 30 to 80% of soil carbon.
Most upland topsoils hold 0.5% to 3.0% organic carbon; below 0.5% is mostly limited to deserts, and above 12–18% soils are classed as organic soils.
Organic carbon builds up where waterlogging slows decomposition so additions outpace losses, as in swamps, bogs and marshes.
Fire-derived charcoal and black carbon occur in most soils, typically supplying 5–50% of organic carbon and more than 50% in mollisols, chernozems and terra preta.

title: Soil organic carbon and soil function
article: Soil carbon#Soil organic carbon and soil function

definition.text: The way organic carbon sustains a soil's ability to provide services, a capacity known as soil health.

facts.text: Carbon benchmarks used to judge soil health include CO2 release, humus levels and microbial metabolic activity.
In sandy soils bulk density falls as organic carbon rises, and bulk density is needed to calculate organic carbon stocks.
Organic carbon raises cation exchange capacity in sandy soils, accounting for up to 76% of its variation in one study.
Organic carbon rises with silt and clay content and is highest in the clay fraction, as fine particles bind decomposing matter into protective aggregates.

title: Soil carbon and climate change
article: Soil carbon#Soil carbon and climate change

definition.text: The two-way link between climate and soil carbon: climate change alters soils and their carbon, and soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate.

facts.text: Changing temperature and moisture alter soil formation, so climate change is likely to affect fertility, salinity, moisture, temperature, organic carbon and aggregation.
Plant uptake fixes carbon dioxide in soil, building a pool of around 1500 Pg in the first few metres, 20-40% of it lasting more than 100 years.
Forest soils are a large carbon pool, and deforestation releases carbon from it that may markedly raise greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
Soil microbes break down soil carbon, and changes in their activity as temperatures rise could contribute to climate change.
In polar regions melting permafrost can expose land to more plant growth and carbon uptake, while in the tropics warmer soils lose aggregation and quality.
Researchers are looking for ways that farming and other human interventions can restore carbon to soils.

title: Managing soil carbon

definition.text: Choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon and to build it up.

facts.text: Exchange of carbon between soils and the atmosphere is a significant part of the global carbon cycle, and humans and farming now affect it most.
Land-use change such as deforestation has caused substantial soil carbon losses, though exact amounts are hard to measure.
Fire strips soil cover and causes immediate and continuing losses of soil organic carbon.
Tillage and drainage expose organic matter to oxygen; peatlands in the Netherlands, East Anglia, Florida and the California Delta have subsided severely as a result.
Grazing that leaves soil bare, through too long or too short recovery periods, also loses soil carbon.
Farmers are discouraged from stubble burning and over-cultivation and encouraged to work in organic material such as manure.
Raising soil carbon is not simple, because soil organisms consume and release carbon and become more active when nitrogen fertilizer is added.

title: Carbon catchment health

definition.text: The wider benefits to soil and catchment health that come from raising soil carbon, beyond its role as a carbon sink.

facts.text: More stable aggregates resist erosion and sedimentation, and soils that keep their strength when wet are less prone to mass movement.
Nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways.
Greater water holding capacity cuts overland flow and keeps water available to plants.
The benefits are hard to quantify because natural resource systems are complex and soil health is open to interpretation.

title: Soil carbon monitoring
article: Soil carbon#Measuring data on soil organic carbon

definition.text: Estimating soil organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling, as climate reporting requires.

facts.text: Under the UN climate convention, countries report changes in five carbon pools, soil carbon among them, following IPCC good practice guidance.
Tanzania, with the FAO, runs a forest soil carbon monitoring programme that combines survey and modelling methods.
For Europe, the European Soil Database gives the most consistent organic carbon data, and one model puts the topsoil stock of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt.
Carbon in Australian farm soils, typically 1.6–4.6% today, may once have been twice as high.

definition.text: The release of carbon from soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to warming.

facts.text: Soils hold roughly two to three times as much carbon as the atmosphere, which makes the feedback crucial for future climate.
Faster soil respiration is the main cause; measurements imply 4 °C of warming raises annual soil respiration by up to 37%.
Global soil respiration rose by about 0.1% a year between 1989 and 2008, most likely because warming sped up decomposition of soil organic matter.
A warming experiment at Harvard, run since 1991, suggests the top metre of soils could release about 190 petagrams of carbon by 2100.
A 2018 study found climate-driven soil carbon losses already occurring across many ecosystems, with a detectable global trend.
Observations of thawing permafrost suggest a linear, chronic release of greenhouse gases as warming continues.
Global decomposition models poorly represent soil animals such as insects and worms and their interactions with microbes.

definition.text: A proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands.

facts.text: It was identified in a 2011 study, whose authors noted a unique stable soil carbon equilibrium for any fixed atmospheric temperature.
Climate models do not account for the heat released by microbes as they decompose organic matter.
Peatlands are predicted to shift from carbon sink to source this century, yet they are still left out of the main Earth system models.

definition.text: A natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere, taking up more carbon than it releases.

facts.text: Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle.
Globally the two most important sinks are vegetation and the ocean, and soil is an important carbon store.
Natural sinks include soil, a carbon store and active sink; land plants during growing seasons; and the ocean through its solubility and biological pumps.
Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground, but no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the atmosphere at large scale.
For greenhouse gases other than CO2 a sink need not store the gas; nitrous oxide, for example, can be reduced to harmless N2.
Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change.
For climate change mitigation, keeping and enhancing natural sinks, mainly soils and forests, is important.

definition.text: Any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time.

facts.text: Carbon pool is the overarching term: pools include the atmosphere, oceans, soil, plants and fossil fuels, and a carbon sink is one type of pool.
Pools and sinks both matter for understanding the carbon cycle, but they mean slightly different things.
Related terms are reservoir, sequestration, source and uptake.

definition.text: The role of soils as a short- to long-term carbon store holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined.

facts.text: Plant litter and other biomass, charcoal included, build up as soil organic matter that weathering and microbes then break down.
Tougher compounds such as cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, waxes and terpenoids are retained together as humus.
Organic matter accumulates in cold regions such as the boreal forests of North America and the Russian taiga.
In tropical and subtropical climates litter and humus are oxidized fast and leached by rain, so slash-and-burn fields stay fertile only two to three years.
Grasslands store organic matter mainly in fibrous root mats, helped by cool, semi-arid to arid climates; natural grass fires also leave stable biochar in the soil.
Since the 1850s much of the world's grassland has been tilled into cropland, rapidly oxidizing large amounts of soil organic carbon.
Intensive farming has severely depleted the organic carbon of many agricultural soils worldwide.
Methods that markedly raise soil carbon storage, such as no-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation, are called carbon farming.

title: Soil carbon sponge

definition.text: Porous, well-aggregated, healthy soil that absorbs and holds water well.

facts.text: The Australian scientist Walter Jehne set out the idea in his 2017 paper Regenerate Earth, linking soil carbon to a restored water cycle that could cool the planet.
A soil carbon sponge is much lighter, about 1 gram/cc, than the parent mineral soil at 2.6–3.5 grams/cc.
Bare soils, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation speed oxidation of soil carbon and shrink the sponge; fire and flooding also harm it.
Afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build the sponge, which also serves as a carbon sink.

notes: Its claims of planetary cooling (S:592b0c50b41c, S:6c5a538a9783) are framed as Jehne's anticipations and postulates, not established findings.

title: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage

definition.text: The part that root-associated mycorrhizal fungi play in building, keeping and losing the soil carbon pool.

facts.text: Mycorrhizal fungi live symbiotically with the roots of almost all plants and are emerging as important to maintaining soil carbon, alongside plants, decomposers and minerals.
Plants send an estimated 5 to 20% of their carbon uptake to these fungi, whose biomass can rival that of fine roots in some ecosystems.
On forested islands in Sweden, mycorrhizal fungi hold 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil.
Their biomass turns over quickly and in some ecosystems is the main route by which living carbon enters the soil carbon pool.
Arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi are phylogenetically distinct and often act in very different ways, so evidence is weighed separately for each.
Their effect on fine root decay is equivocal: ectomycorrhizal colonization speeds it in some ecosystems but slows it in Pinus edulis roots.

title: Recalcitrance of mycorrhizal tissues
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Recalcitrance of mycorrhizal tissues

definition.text: The idea that how slowly mycorrhizal fungal tissue decays helps set how long its carbon stays in soil.

facts.text: Glomalin, made only by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, accumulates in some soils and may be a substantial share of their carbon.
Later experiments found arbuscular fungi cause net soil carbon losses, and proteomics showed most glomalin-extracted proteins are not mycorrhizal, so its role is likely overestimated.
Chitin was thought to slow decay of ectomycorrhizal tissue, but Fernandez and Koide (2012) found it does not decompose more slowly than other compounds.

contested_note: Whether glomalin adds much to soil carbon is disputed: early work reported large stores, while later experiments and protein analyses suggest the contribution is overestimated.

title: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil aggregation
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Effects on soil aggregation

definition.text: The way mycorrhizal fungi help bind soil into aggregates that physically shield organic carbon from microbial decay.

facts.text: Because aggregates protect organic carbon from soil microbes, more aggregate formation can mean more soil carbon storage.
Much evidence shows arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase aggregate formation, possibly through the protein glomalin.
Even if glomalin itself decays readily, it may still store carbon by promoting aggregates that protect other organic matter.
Ectomycorrhizal fungi have only anecdotal links to aggregation in sand bags, with no evidence yet that they aid aggregates in field soils.

title: Mycorrhizal priming
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Stimulation of decomposition (priming)

definition.text: The speeding-up of soil carbon decomposition when mycorrhizal fungi feed free-living decomposers with easily used carbon compounds.

facts.text: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been shown to increase soil carbon decomposition in nutrient-rich patches.
Since they are thought to lack the enzymes to do this themselves, they are believed to stimulate decomposers by exuding labile energy substrates.
Lab experiments show soils with arbuscular fungi lose more carbon than soils without them, and the gap widens under elevated CO2.
Evidence for ectomycorrhizal priming is inconclusive: field data suggest faster carbon loss, but lab tests show root exudation falls as ectomycorrhizal colonization rises.

title: Mycorrhizal inhibition of decomposition
article: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage#Inhibition of decomposition

definition.text: The slowing of soil carbon decomposition when ectomycorrhizal fungi compete with free-living decomposers for nutrients or water.

facts.text: The first report, in 1971, came from Pinus radiata plantations in New Zealand, where excluding roots and their fungi led to net carbon loss.
Several later studies found ectomycorrhizal fungi reduce decomposer activity and so increase soil carbon storage.
A theoretical model shows that fungal access to organic nitrogen should slow decomposition by leaving decomposers nutrient-limited.
Koide and Wu (2003) argued that competition for soil water may matter more than competition for nutrients.

title: Enhanced weathering

definition.text: A carbon dioxide removal method that speeds up natural weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so that it reacts with water and air.

facts.text: Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 from the atmosphere and stores it permanently in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity.
Methods are land-based, such as in-situ carbonation of silicates, or ocean-based; ultramafic rock could store hundreds to thousands of years' worth of CO2 emissions.
Mine tailings and alkaline industrial wastes such as steel slag or biomass ash could serve first, though more basalt mining might eventually be needed.
Mixing crushed silicate rock into soil can benefit plant health as well as carbon sequestration when calcium or magnesium is present.
In July 2020 a group of scientists judged that spreading finely crushed basalt on fields has potential for national carbon dioxide removal.
A 2020 analysis put its cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2, comparable to BECCS (US$100–200) and direct air capture (US$100–300).
It could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year, with cost estimates in the US$50–200 per tonne range.

title: Silicate weathering and carbon dioxide
article: Enhanced weathering#Natural mineral weathering and ocean acidification

definition.text: The natural removal of atmospheric CO2 when carbonic acid in rain and groundwater dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals.

facts.text: For silicate weathering, theory gives 1 mol of CO2 sequestered for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+ released, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure.
Carbonate weathering followed by carbonate precipitation sequesters no net CO2.
Dissolved bicarbonate travels through soil and groundwater to the ocean, where organisms build carbonate shells; over geological time this is thought to stabilize climate.
The reactions reverse when carbonate meets acids, as in soils; liming acid soils neutralizes hydrogen ions but releases CO2 from the limestone.

notes: S:13a7136f7fa0 carries a CLARIFICATION NEEDED tag.

title: Terrestrial enhanced weathering

definition.text: Enhanced weathering done on land by spreading crushed silicate minerals over the ground surface.

facts.text: How fast the rock dissolves depends on its reactive surface area, the pH and buffer capacity of the receiving soil and soil biological activity, though rates remain uncertain.
Weathering slows as the soil solution saturates, so some argue low rainfall limits it, while others say new minerals or plant uptake keep weathering going.
The energy needed to grind the rock depends on how quickly it dissolves.
A 2012 study found a wide range of possible costs, mostly because dissolution rates are uncertain.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether low rainfall limits the weathering of rock spread on land.

definition.text: The deliberate dissolution and carbonation of silicate minerals to lock CO2 into carbonate.

facts.text: It was first proposed by Seifritz in 1990 and developed by Lackner and colleagues and the Albany Research Center.
Early work reacted crushed silicates at about 180 °C and 15 MPa of CO2 in reactors; in-situ methods inject CO2 into silicate rock formations instead.
Research has mostly targeted CO2 from flue gas, but with CO2 taken from the air it could serve as geoengineering.
Soil remineralization with crushed rock contributes to the same enhanced weathering process.

title: Permafrost zones

definition.text: The division of permafrost regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost: continuous, discontinuous, sporadic and isolated.

facts.text: In the continuous zone 90%–100% of land is underlain by permafrost, in the discontinuous zone 50%–90%, and in the sporadic zone 10%–50%; isolated patches cover 10% or less.
About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's ice-free land is directly underlain by permafrost, but 22% lies within a permafrost zone.
Permafrost usually forms wherever mean annual air temperature is below freezing, except in humid boreal forests where snow insulates the ground.
Where the mean annual soil surface temperature is between −5 and 0 °C, permafrost usually stays discontinuous, forming only in sheltered spots.
Below −5 °C slope aspect can never thaw it, and a continuous permafrost zone (CPZ) forms.
Soil scientists abbreviate the sporadic zone SPZ and the extensive discontinuous zone DPZ.

title: Alpine permafrost

definition.text: Permafrost found at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year.

facts.text: Extensive alpine permafrost generally needs a mean annual air temperature of −3 °C, though some mountains hold it at −1 °C.
It is hard to study, and systematic research began only in the 1970s; in 2009 permafrost was even found on Mount Kilimanjaro.
Regional estimates collected in 2014 put its global extent at 3,560,000 km2, with the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau the largest area at 1,300,000 km2.
Subsurface alpine permafrost can lie beneath warmer soil that supports vegetation.

title: Subsea permafrost

definition.text: Permafrost beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves, on land exposed during the Last Glacial Maximum and since flooded.

facts.text: It formed on land during the last Ice Age, when sea levels were low, and has slowly declined since being submerged under warmer, saltier conditions.
Today it covers an estimated 2 million km2, about a fifth of the land permafrost domain and 30–50% less than at the Last Glacial Maximum.
It holds around 560 GtC in organic matter and 45 GtC as methane, releasing 18 and 38 MtC a year in a millennial-scale response to post-glacial warming.
Under RCP 8.5 it could release 43 GtC by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300, though human-driven effects will show only after hundreds or thousands of years.

title: Past extent of permafrost

definition.text: The much larger area that permafrost covered during the Last Glacial Maximum.

facts.text: Continuous permafrost then covered all of ice-free Europe south to about Szeged in Hungary, and East Asia south to present-day Changchun.
In North America only a narrow belt lay south of the ice sheet, but it reached the southern borders of Idaho and Oregon in the drier west.
In the Southern Hemisphere there is evidence of former, probably discontinuous permafrost in central Otago and Argentine Patagonia.

title: Permafrost base depth

definition.text: The depth at which Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C, marking the bottom of permafrost.

facts.text: Base depth ranges from less than a meter to 1,493 m in the northern Lena and Yana River basins of Siberia.
Permafrost forms much more slowly after the first few metres: at Prudhoe Bay it reaches 4.44 m after 1 year but 687.7 m only after 775,000 years.
The deep permafrost at Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, took over half a million years to form, spanning several Pleistocene glacial cycles.
Permafrost in soil conducts heat less well than in bedrock, so it is less affected by the geothermal gradient.

title: Massive ground ice

definition.text: Permafrost so rich in ice that ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass.

facts.text: Massive icy beds are at least 2 m thick and 10 m across, and range from icy mud to pure ice.
Of the four kinds of ground ice, pore ice, ice wedges, buried surface ice and intrasedimental ice, only the last two grow large enough to count as massive.
Segregational ice, the main intrasedimental type, forms as water migrates to the freezing front, mostly in silts of low salinity.
Forming it in the top 2.5 m takes 1–1000 years in clay, 10–10,000 years in peat and 1,000–1,000,000 years in silt.

title: Permafrost landforms

definition.text: The surface features built by freezing, cracking and thawing of permafrost ground.

facts.text: Thermal contraction cracks that become ice wedges, and solifluction downslope, create polygons, rings, steps and other patterned ground.
Melting ground ice in ice-rich permafrost starts thermokarst landforms: thermokarst lakes, thaw slumps, thermal-erosion gullies and active layer detachments.
Meltwater trapped over deep permafrost in Arctic bogs freezes into ice lenses that push the ground up into mounds.
These grow into palsas, peat mounds 15–150 m long but under 6 m tall, and larger pingos, 3–70 m high and up to 1,000 m across.

title: Permafrost ecology

definition.text: How permanently frozen ground shapes the plants, animals and microbes that live with it.

facts.text: Only shallow-rooted plants survive over permafrost; black spruce tolerates limited rooting zones and dominates where permafrost is extensive.
Frozen permafrost soil still holds microorganisms, typically from 1 to 1000 million per gram.
Most permafrost bacteria and fungi cannot be cultured in the lab, so they are identified by DNA-based techniques.
Living permafrost microbes show adaptations to sub-zero conditions, including reduced and anaerobic metabolism.

title: Construction on permafrost

definition.text: Engineering methods for building on permafrost without thawing the frozen ground that supports the structure.

facts.text: Heat from a building or pipeline can thaw the soil, and as ice turns to water the ground loses its ability to support the structure.
Norilsk and Yakutsk, both in Russia, are the only two large cities built on continuous permafrost.
Wood pile foundations, pioneered by Mikhail Kim in Norilsk, should reach 15 metres, where the temperature stays at about −5 °C all year.
Other methods are gravel pads 1–2 m thick and ammonia heat pipes, as in the supports of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

title: Permafrost thaw

definition.text: The warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground.

facts.text: Permafrost warmed globally by about 0.3 °C between 2007 and 2016, more in the continuous zone than the discontinuous zone.
Warming reached up to 3 °C in parts of Northern Alaska from the early 1980s to mid-2000s, and up to 2 °C in the Russian European North from 1970 to 2020.
Average active layer thickness rose from ~127 centimetres to ~145 centimetres between 2000 and 2018, about ~0.65 centimetres a year.
In Yukon the continuous permafrost zone may have moved 100 kilometres poleward since 1899, though accurate records span only 30 years.
Model projections, process understanding and paleoclimate evidence make it virtually certain that permafrost will keep shrinking as climate warms.
The volume of permafrost in the upper 3 m is expected to fall by about 25% per 1 °C of global warming.

title: Permafrost carbon feedback

definition.text: The warming caused when thawing permafrost releases its stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, which in turn drives more thaw.

facts.text: Northern circumpolar permafrost holds organic matter equal to 1400–1650 billion tons of carbon, about twice the carbon in the atmosphere.
Most of it, ~1,035 billion tons, lies in near-surface permafrost no deeper than 3 metres, but only a fraction is expected to reach the atmosphere.
Even under the RCP8.5 scenario of over 4 °C warming, about 5% to 15% of permafrost carbon is expected to be lost over decades and centuries.
Aerobic respiration releases CO2 and anaerobic respiration methane; methane will be a small share of the carbon yet cause 40–70% of the 21st-century warming from thaw.
Arctic greening will offset some emissions, but very unlikely all of them, while more Arctic wildfires can speed permafrost carbon release.
The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases equal to 14–175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per 1 °C of warming.
There is widespread agreement that permafrost emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small to cause runaway warming.
Gradual thaw would add around 0.09 °C by 2100 if warming is held to 2 °C; abrupt collapse near 4 °C of warming could add 0.2–0.4 °C.

contested_note: Whether permafrost thaw is a global tipping point is debated: thaw is self-perpetuating locally, but in aggregate it proceeds gradually with warming.

title: Thaw-induced ground instability

definition.text: The weakening and movement of ground as its permafrost ice thaws and drains.

facts.text: As meltwater drains or evaporates, soil structure weakens and can turn viscous; trees tilting at random, so-called drunken trees, are a visible sign.
Warming has increased slope disturbances on permafrost, sharply raising sediment loads in rivers, and thaw can also drain and dry northern wetlands.
In high mountains thaw reduces slope stability by building pore-water pressure, leading to slope failure and rockfalls such as the 1987 Val Pola landslide.
Thaw also forms frozen debris lobes, slow landslides of soil, rock, trees and ice; 43 were identified in Alaska's southern Brooks Range by December 2021.

title: Permafrost thaw and infrastructure

definition.text: The threat that thawing permafrost poses to settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings built on frozen ground.

facts.text: As of 2021, 1162 settlements with about 5 million people sit on Arctic permafrost, and the permafrost below 42% of them is expected to thaw by 2050.
By 2050 nearly 70% of infrastructure in permafrost areas could be at high risk, including 30–50% of critical infrastructure, at costs of tens of billions of dollars.
In Alaska alone, damages by 2100 would reach $4.6 billion under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario.
The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is warming at twice the global rate, 40% of its permafrost is already warm, and around 30% of its roads are damaged.

title: Pollutants released by permafrost thaw

definition.text: Toxic waste and natural mercury held in frozen ground that thaw could release into the environment.

facts.text: For much of the 20th century permafrost was thought to preserve buried material indefinitely, so it became a popular site for hazardous waste disposal.
About 4500 industrial facilities handle hazardous chemicals in Arctic permafrost areas, and 13,000 to 20,000 heavily contaminated sites, 70% in Russia, are trapped in it.
An estimated 800,000 tons of mercury are frozen in permafrost soil; around 70% is taken up by vegetation after thaw.
Under RCP8.5, enough mercury would reach the Yukon River basin by 2050 to make its fish unsafe to eat under EPA guidelines.

title: Revival of ancient organisms from permafrost

definition.text: The survival of ancient microbes and plant tissue in frozen ground, and their possible revival when permafrost thaws.

facts.text: Dormant bacteria and inactive viruses have raised concerns that thaw could free unknown pathogens of humans, livestock or crops.
Others note that pathogens such as influenza and smallpox seem unable to survive thawing, and a review describes the risks as generally low.
In 2012 Russian researchers revived Silene stenophylla from 30,000-year-old tissue in an Ice Age squirrel burrow, the oldest plant tissue ever revived.

contested_note: Scientists disagree on whether microbes freed by thaw could survive and threaten people; a scientific review rates the risk generally low.

title: History of permafrost research

definition.text: The development of permafrost science from early Siberian reports to modern international collaboration.

facts.text: One of the earliest reports dates to 1684, when permafrost stopped well digging in Yakutsk; until the mid-20th century most of the literature was in Russian.
Karl Ernst von Baer, often called the founder of scientific permafrost research, published from 1838 and wrote the first permafrost textbook in 1843.
Siemon William Muller's 1943 report coined the English word permafrost from permanently frozen ground, translating the Russian vechnaia merzlota.
The First International Conference on Permafrost met at Purdue University in November 1963, and the International Permafrost Association was created in 1983.

title: Active layer

definition.text: The top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn.

facts.text: Soil temperature is steadier at depth than at the surface, so seasonal heating and cooling fade with depth.
In winter a frost front forms in the soil, and in spring and summer the soil thaws from the top down.
Where summer heat cannot thaw the soil completely, permafrost forms; the year-round frozen soil below the active layer is the inactive layer.
The boundary between the active layer and permafrost is sometimes called the permafrost table.
Water cannot drain below the active layer, so permafrost lands tend to be very poorly drained and boggy.
In 2018 it averaged ~145 centimetres in the Northern Hemisphere, under 50 centimetres in northeastern Siberia, Alaska and Greenland and over 600 centimetres in southern Norway and Mongolia.
Roots cannot grow below the active layer, so continuous permafrost restricts trees to shallow-rooted species such as larch.

title: Thaw depth

definition.text: The level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, separating thawed soil from frozen soil below.

facts.text: The active layer thickness is the maximum thaw depth over two years.
Maximum air temperature is the main control: the active layer is only 10 cm on Ellesmere Island, about 2.5 m at Yakutsk and 5 meters at Yellowknife.
Coarse sandy or gravelly parent material conducts heat better, giving active layers up to five times deeper than in loam- or clay-rich material.
Vegetation and soil organic matter alter bulk density and so thermal conductivity; thaw depth matters for both ecology and construction.

title: Soil formation in the active layer
article: Active layer#Soil formation in the active layer

definition.text: The cold-climate soil-forming processes, dominated by frost churning, that act in the seasonally thawed layer above permafrost.

facts.text: Cryoturbation dominates and tends to make the active layer uniform in composition.
Yet soils vary markedly with parent rock, because weathering is so slow in the very cold climate.
Slow decomposition makes gelisols, the permafrost soils, an important sink for carbon dioxide.
This stored carbon means permafrost thaw may accelerate global warming, especially if the carbon predates the recent glacial maxima.

title: Pereletok

definition.text: A layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws.

facts.text: The Russian word means that which survives over the summer; it is also called intergelisol.
Frozen ground is sometimes split into permafrost, pereletok and seasonally frozen ground by how long it stays frozen.
Pereletok can be seen as part of the active layer that stays frozen after an unusually cool summer or cold winter.
The line between pereletok and permafrost is not universally defined and is hard to draw in the field.

definition.text: A zone of ground that stays unfrozen all year within a permafrost area.

facts.text: In continuous permafrost, taliks often lie under shallow thermokarst lakes and rivers whose deep water does not freeze in winter.
They are classed as closed, open or through, depending on whether permafrost surrounds them, they open at the top, or they also connect to unfrozen ground below the permafrost.
One study suggests open taliks are more widespread in fault zones and near large rivers.

definition.text: An unfrozen layer that forms between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost when summer-thawed ground fails to refreeze in winter.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary taliks, which are usually tied to water bodies, it results from climate warming.
Warming produces it in moderately cold regions; colder regions just thaw deeper in summer, and warm, shallow permafrost simply disappears.
With rising air temperature or snow depth the talik thickens until the deep permafrost vanishes.
This type of talik has recently been observed in Russia.

definition.text: Ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass with 50–90% ice by volume.

facts.text: It covers more than one million square kilometers from northeast Siberia to Alaska and Canada, in many places tens of meters thick.
It forms in poorly drained, severely cold lowlands with ice wedge polygons, sparse vegetation, intense periglacial weathering and nearby sediment sources.
It may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, a multiple of yearly fossil fuel emissions.
Thawing yedoma is a significant methane source, about 4 Tg of CH4 per year.
At the end of the last ice age, thawing yedoma and its thermokarst lakes may have produced 33 to 87% of the high-latitude rise in atmospheric methane.

title: Thermokarst

definition.text: Irregular terrain of marshy hollows and small hummocks formed when ice-rich permafrost thaws.

facts.text: It occurs in Arctic areas and on a smaller scale in mountains such as the Himalayas and Swiss Alps; the name comes from its resemblance to limestone karst.
Thermokarst lakes form in thaw depressions in permafrost with over 30% ice by volume, and tend to form and drain in a cycle.
Thaw lakes warm the ground beneath them, so permafrost below is shallower and a talik is present under deep enough lakes.
Forming thaw lakes is a positive feedback, releasing methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from thawing permafrost.

title: Permafrost carbon cycle

definition.text: The Arctic part of the global carbon cycle, in which carbon moves from permafrost soils to plants, microbes and the air and back into frozen soil by burial.

facts.text: Carbon returns to permafrost soils through burial and sedimentation by cryogenic processes, while some passes to the ocean and the wider global cycle.
It includes exchanges of carbon dioxide and methane with the air and transfers to water as dissolved and particulate organic and inorganic carbon.
Permafrost-affected soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land yet store between 25 and 50% of the soil organic carbon.
Because permafrost responds slowly to climate, it keeps carbon out of the air for long periods; radiocarbon dating shows much of it is thousands of years old.
This large reservoir was often neglected in early carbon estimates and climate models, but research on it has grown enormously since the 2000s.
Microbial respiration is the main route by which old permafrost carbon re-enters the air, its rate set by soil temperature, moisture, nutrients and oxygen.
Iron oxides can hold back microbial respiration, and iron and aluminum can adsorb freed carbon before it escapes, especially in the sandy layers often over permafrost.
Despite the large stores, the whole pool is unlikely to mobilize, because much permafrost will stay frozen even as thaw deepens.

definition.text: The two processes, syngenetic permafrost growth and cryoturbation, that carry plant-derived carbon down into permafrost for storage.

facts.text: Permafrost makes no carbon itself; organic carbon from plants must enter the soil and then be incorporated into the frozen ground.
In syngenetic growth the surface rises by wind or river sediment or peat, up to 0.5mm/yr for peat and 0.7mm/yr for sediment, burying carbon into permafrost.
Cryoturbation, mixing by freeze–thaw cycles and most often frost heaving, moves surface carbon down until it is incorporated into permafrost.
Storage rates increase when cryoturbation and sediment deposition act together.

title: Permafrost carbon stocks

definition.text: The amount of organic carbon held in permafrost-region soils and deposits, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Soil organic carbon in the northern circumpolar permafrost region is estimated at around 1,460–1,600 Pg; with the Tibetan Plateau, Northern Hemisphere permafrost holds around 1832 Gt.
By depth, the top 0–30 cm holds about 200 Pg, the top 0–100 cm about 500 Pg and the top 0–300 cm about 1024 Pg of organic carbon.
These estimates more than doubled the carbon previously known in permafrost soils.
Yedoma (400 Pg) and Arctic deltaic deposits (240 Pg) add more carbon, generally deeper than the 3 m of traditional studies.
In 2003 Tarnocai and colleagues estimated carbon stocks in cryosols, soils with permafrost within two meters of the surface, from the Northern and Mid Latitudes Soil Database.

title: Permafrost carbon release
article: Permafrost carbon cycle#Carbon release from the permafrost

definition.text: The escape of long-stored carbon from thawing permafrost soils to the atmosphere as microbes decompose it.

facts.text: Arctic warming deepens the active layer, exposing carbon stored for decades to millennia to microbial processes that release it into the air.
Warming also intensifies the Arctic water cycle, and more warm rain deepens thaw further.
How much is released depends on thaw depth, the carbon content of thawed soil, physical change and microbial and plant activity.
Once thawed, ground will not return to permafrost for centuries even if warming reverses.
A 1993 study found the tundra had been a carbon sink until the late 1970s but had since become a net carbon source.
The 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated net release of 0.3 to 0.6 Pg C a year, winter emissions exceeding growing-season uptake by vegetation.
A 2022 study of atmospheric records from 1980 to 2017 challenged this, finding permafrost regions had been gaining carbon on net.
Methane lasts under 12 years in the air but warms around 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years, so the gas released matters as much as the carbon amount.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether permafrost regions are already a net carbon source: the 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated a net release, while a 2022 study of atmospheric records found a net gain.

conflicts.text: Methane's global warming potential is about 28 times larger than that of CO2 over a 100-year period.

title: Permafrost carbon dioxide emissions

definition.text: The carbon dioxide released by aerobic microbial respiration in thawed permafrost soils, the bulk of permafrost emissions.

facts.text: Most permafrost soils are oxic, so carbon dioxide makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost and Arctic emissions.
Early 2020s studies show soil microbes respire mostly modern carbon in the growing season but live on ancient carbon in winter.
Plants on thawed ground root deeper, grow larger and take up more carbon, generally the main counteracting feedback.
Wildfires on thawed land burn off the insulating organic mat, warming the soil and deepening the active layer.

contested_note: Researchers debate whether rising permafrost emissions come mainly from ancient frozen carbon or from faster respiration of modern plant litter in warmer soils.

title: Permafrost methane emissions

definition.text: The methane produced by anaerobic microbes in waterlogged thawed permafrost, especially under thermokarst lakes.

facts.text: Methanogenesis needs thoroughly anaerobic conditions, so it centres on Arctic lakes, where 2022 observations show at least half of the methane made reaches the air.
A 2015 review found anaerobic sites emitted 75–85% less than aerobic ones, but a 2018 incubation study found methane matched CO2 once methanogens were established.
A 2017 paper found that less than 10% of methane from thawing peatlands came from old, thawed carbon, the rest from decomposition of modern carbon.
Peatland methane from thaw starts high, at 82 milligrams per square meter per day, then falls nearly threefold as the permafrost bog matures.

contested_note: The sources call the rate and trajectory of methane production in thawed permafrost a matter of continuing scientific debate.

title: Abrupt permafrost thaw

definition.text: Rapid thaw by hillside collapse (retrogressive thaw slumps) and thermokarst lake formation, which can expose deep soil to microbes within days.

facts.text: After a 2020 Siberian heatwave, thaw slumps on the northern Taymyr Peninsula rose 17-fold, from 82 to 1404, and soil carbon mobilization 28-fold.
Abrupt thaw adds between 60 and 100 gigatonnes of carbon by 2300, raising emissions by ~125–190% over gradual thaw alone.
It often raises the share of methane over carbon dioxide, a major source of uncertainty in projections of permafrost methane.
Climate models long focused on gradual thaw because abrupt thaw is hard to model.
In 2019, three permafrost sites expected to stay frozen for 70 more years under the intermediate RCP4.5 pathway had already thawed abruptly.
Methane from peatlands after thaw starts high, 82 milligrams per square metre per day, but falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

title: Permafrost emission estimates

definition.text: Projections of the total greenhouse gases that thawing permafrost will release over this century and beyond.

facts.text: Preliminary 2011 analyses put permafrost emissions at around 15% of human emissions, but could not account for abrupt thaw.
A 2020 study found northern permafrost peatlands, 3.7 of the 18 million km2, would cause ~1% of human radiative forcing by 2100 and become net carbon sinks within 200 years.
A 2021 estimate including abrupt thaw gave 150–200 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2100 at 1.5 °C of warming, 220–300 at 2 °C and 400–500 above 4 °C.
A 2022 assessment found abrupt thaw adds 50% to gradual rates, 14 billion tons of CO2 equivalent by 2100 per degree of warming.

title: Effects of climate change on agriculture
article: Effects of climate change on agriculture

definition.text: The many ways a changing climate alters farming, most of them making it harder for agriculture to provide global food security.

facts.text: Climate change is likely to worsen farming's environmental impacts by lowering productivity, weakening agrochemicals and increasing soil erosion and pests.
Drought, heat waves and flooding lower crop yields; one study linked 1°C of warming to a 3 to 7% fall in global yields of major staple crops.
Effects on land include coastal farmland lost to sea level rise, new arable land as frozen ground thaws, more erosion and changes in soil fertility and growing seasons.
CO2 fertilization offsets a small part of the harm but lowers essential micronutrients in crops and does little for C4 crops like maize.
The future extent of soil erosion and groundwater depletion are among the main uncertainties.
Adaptation can come through management practices, agricultural innovation, institutional change and climate-smart agriculture.

title: Climate change and soil fertility
article: Effects of climate change on agriculture#Erosion and soil fertility

definition.text: The decline in soil quality expected as warming brings heavier rain and faster decay of soil organic matter.

facts.text: A more vigorous water cycle with extreme rainfall makes erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely; erosion can strip up to 22% of soil carbon in 50 years.
Warmer soils decompose organic matter faster, lowering soil organic carbon and the soil's ability to hold nutrients and water.
Soil microbe populations could rise 40–150%, and warmth would favour certain bacteria, shifting community composition.
Elevated carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth, slowing the soil carbon cycle and favouring slow-growing, efficient oligotrophs over copiotrophs.

title: Agricultural greenhouse gas emissions

definition.text: The greenhouse gases released by farming, including from agricultural soils and from clearing land for crops.

facts.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Direct emissions come from rice and livestock farming, and indirect ones from converting forests and other land to farmland.
Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of direct agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.
Emissions from farm soils depend on soil type, climate and management; conservation tillage, precision agriculture, better water use and biochar can cut them and store soil carbon.
Deforestation, rice methane, cattle methane and fertilizer nitrous oxide together make up 54% of methane emissions, about 80% of nitrous oxide emissions and nearly all land-use CO2.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer gives about 5% of human greenhouse emissions, two thirds of it during use, as soil bacteria turn nitrate into nitrous oxide.
Long-flooded rice soils cannot take in oxygen, so organic matter ferments to methane; better water management, such as wetting and drying, can cut this by up to 90%.
Reduced tillage, returning crop residues to the soil and more cover crops can lower farm carbon dioxide emissions.

title: Climate change mitigation

definition.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change, also called decarbonisation.

facts.text: Mitigation actions include conserving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy sources.
An important measure is preserving and enhancing carbon sinks, managing them so they remove more CO2 and store it durably; scientists also call this carbon sequestration.
The 2022 IPCC report calls land-based options AFOLU mitigation options, with an economic potential of 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.
Almost 20% of greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture and forestry; cutting nitrogen fertilizer use could avoid nitrous oxide equal to 2.77 - 11.48 gigatons of CO2 from 2020 to 2050.

title: Soil carbon sequestration

definition.text: Drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon; it is a major soil property and an ecosystem service.

facts.text: There are many measures to raise soil carbon, which makes it hard to measure and account for, but they carry fewer trade-offs than BECCS or afforestation.
Protecting healthy soils and restoring the soil carbon sponge could remove 7.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, more than annual US emissions.
Farming can deplete soil carbon, but conservation farming can protect it and repair the damage over time.
Methods include cover crops, no-till farming, residue mulching and crop rotation.
Best practices for European soils are converting arable land to grassland, straw incorporation, reduced tillage, ley cropping and cover crops.
Trees exude more carbon below ground than they capture above it, helping build a soil carbon sponge.
Biochar retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years.
Rattan Lal's 2004 Science paper on soil carbon sequestration was the first to report that restoring soil organic matter both improves soil health and reduces atmospheric CO2.

notes: Claims for grazing-based sequestration are disputed in the sources (Allan Savory, e.g. S:2500c9f77f25); that debate is drafted as Grazing management and soil carbon in the fertilizers chapter.

definition.text: Restoring wetlands and peatlands so that they keep sequestering carbon and storing water.

facts.text: It has moderate to great mitigation potential on limited land, with low trade-offs and costs; wetlands store about 45 million tonnes of carbon a year.
Some wetlands are significant sources of methane, and some also emit nitrous oxide.
Peatland covers just 3% of the land surface but stores up to 550 gigatonnes of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon.
Peatlands are threatened by drainage for farming, logging and peat sales for compost; blocking drainage channels lets natural vegetation recover.

title: Pingo

definition.text: An ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost.

facts.text: Pingos are typically conical periglacial landforms; more than 11,000 exist, the most, 1,350, on the Tuktoyaktuk peninsula.

Closed-system pingos form in continuous permafrost as an infilled lake freezes and squeezes trapped water upward; open-system pingos are fed by artesian groundwater, often in thin discontinuous permafrost.
They grow a couple of centimetres a year, and when their ice core melts they collapse into depressions that show permafrost once existed.
John Franklin first described one in 1825; in 1938 Alf Erling Porsild borrowed the Inuvialuit word, meaning conical hill, for scientific use.

notes: Image: a photograph of a pingo such as Ibyuk Pingo.

definition.text: Growth of permafrost upward as new material is deposited on a site under freezing conditions.

facts.text: It is an efficient mode of growth compared with heterogenetic growth, in which cold penetrates previously unfrozen ground of uniform composition.
The new material comes from river sediment, debris fallen from hillsides, wind-blown material and lake-bottom deposits.
It is one of the two main processes that store carbon in permafrost, burying organic and mineral soil as the permafrost surface rises.
Ice wedges growing upward into permafrost cracks can count as syngenetic; studies draw on the permafrost tunnel near Fairbanks, Alaska.

title: Black carbon in soils

definition.text: Fire-derived carbon, from vegetation fires or deposited from the air, held in soil as charcoal particles and soot.

facts.text: Black carbon typically makes up 1 to 6%, and up to 60%, of the organic carbon stored in soils.
In tropical soils it serves as a reservoir of nutrients, and soils without much black carbon are significantly less fertile.
Terra preta soils of central Amazonia, rich in black carbon, average three times more soil organic matter than surrounding soils.
Slash-and-burn adds black carbon to soil, but slash-and-char would avoid high emissions of CO2 and volatile black carbon.

conflicts.text: Soil organic carbon is typically 5–50% derived from char, with levels above 50% in mollisol, chernozem and terra preta soils.

definition.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Its two main types are biological sequestration (biosequestration) and geological sequestration.
Biological sequestration captures CO2 by living processes such as photosynthesis, and land-use and farming changes that speed it up are called carbon farming.
It is sometimes confused with carbon capture and storage, which separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed.
Biological stores may be temporary: wildfire, disease, economic pressure and politics can release their carbon again.
Mineral sequestration locks carbon in insoluble carbonate salts for thousands to millions of years.
Converting natural or semi-natural land to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30-40%, and soil carbon keeps changing until a new equilibrium is reached.
Leaving residues, using manure and adding perennial crops, with their larger below-ground biomass, raise carbon input to soil.
About 70% of soil organic carbon outside permafrost lies deeper within the upper metre, stabilized by mineral-organic associations.

conflicts.text: 14.5% of the world's soil carbon is found in wetlands, on 5.5% of land.
conflicts.note: The same page also gives 20-30% of soil carbon on 5-8% of land (S:647216761dcb).

definition.text: Natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions; positive feedbacks amplify warming and negative ones damp it.

facts.text: Calling a feedback positive or negative does not mean it is good or bad.
The sum of feedbacks is negative but becoming less so, so warming will accelerate if emissions continue at current levels.
Physical feedbacks include less reflective snow and ice and more water vapour; biological ones mostly involve how fast plants take up CO2 in the carbon cycle.
The carbon cycle absorbs more than half of yearly CO2 emissions into plants and the ocean, but that share will fall as sinks saturate and drought and wildfire increase.
Methane from land, especially wetlands, and nitrous oxide from land and oceans are a known positive feedback.
Carbon cycle feedbacks are uncertain, and permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane in ways that are hard to model.
The IPCC estimates permafrost could release the equivalent of 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 °C of warming.

definition.text: The positive and negative climate feedbacks that come from Earth's carbon cycle, mostly negative so far.

facts.text: Land and ocean sinks absorb around half of current emissions; the fraction could rise to three-quarters if emissions fall, or drop to one-third by 2100 if they rise.
If emissions stay very high after the 21st century, land ecosystems would become a net carbon source.
Through CO2 fertilization, more CO2 raises plant productivity, and plants lose less water through their stomata.
Chemical weathering removes CO2 over the geological long term and is increasing with current warming.

title: Arctic methane emissions

definition.text: Methane released in the Arctic, mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, clathrate breakdown and the melting Greenland ice sheet, which adds to atmospheric methane.

facts.text: It is a positive climate feedback: thaw exposes organic material to methanogenesis, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas.
Permafrost holds almost twice as much carbon as the atmosphere, with about 20 Gt of permafrost-associated methane trapped in clathrates.
A 2024 assessment put Arctic-Boreal land emissions at about 48.7 Tg of methane a year, with marine sources adding about 4.9 Tg.
Methanogenesis needs fully anaerobic conditions; a 2015 review found anaerobic thaw sites emitted 75-85% less in total than aerobic ones.
A 2018 seven-year incubation found methane production matched CO2 once methanogenic microbes became established at anaerobic sites.
Thermokarst lakes are frequent methane sources, and at least half the methane made in them reaches the atmosphere.
Radiocarbon dating suggests 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon was released as methane and CO2 over the last 60 years.
No evidence ties the Arctic to the methane rise since about 2018, which points to tropical wetlands, but its role will very likely grow.

contested_note: Scientists still debate the rate and trajectory of methane production in thawed permafrost.

definition.text: A controlled, intermittent irrigation method for lowland rice in which fields are allowed to dry for a few days before being re-flooded, instead of being kept under standing water.

facts.text: In 'safe' AWD a perforated tube shows the water table; when it falls 15 cm below the soil surface the field is re-flooded to 5 cm, and it stays flooded at flowering.

Letting the water drop below the surface periodically ends the anaerobic conditions that produce methane; seasonal CH4 emissions fell by up to 85%, and the 2006 IPCC methodology assumes an average 48% cut.
It saves about 38% of water without harming yields, and periodic soil drying lowers arsenic and cadmium in the grain.
Its main drawback is higher nitrous oxide emissions; it suits areas where soils can be drained in 5-day intervals, mainly in the dry season.

title: Biochar permanence

definition.text: How long the carbon locked in biochar stays stored before returning to the atmosphere, the key measure of its durability as carbon removal.

facts.text: Multi-pool models give biochar in soil a centennial to millennial turnover, depending on feedstock, production conditions, application rate and site.
Biochar made above 600 °C resembles the stable coal maceral inertinite; under certain conditions 97% of its organic carbon is highly refractory.
For biochar made at 350–800 °C the labile carbon fraction falls from about 16% to 1%, and incubation experiments have mostly measured the decay of that fraction.
Some studies report sub-centennial turnover, but re-analysis finds the common two-pool decay model badly parameterised, so permanence is generally underestimated.

contested_note: Some studies report biochar turnover within a century, while re-analyses argue that the decay models behind those estimates are flawed and permanence is underestimated.

definition.text: Certified credits sold for carbon dioxide removed by producing biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets.

facts.text: Because abatement costs are high, biochar credits trade at prices an order of magnitude above credits from emission reductions.
In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases.
Standards such as the European Biochar Certificate list permissible feedstocks, and certified suppliers must be carbon net-negative.

title: Pathways of wetland methane emission
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Pathways of methane emission

definition.text: The three routes by which methane made in wetland soils reaches the air: molecular diffusion, transport through plant aerenchyma, and ebullition.

facts.text: The water table marks the boundary between anaerobic methane production below and aerobic methane consumption above; a low water table forces methane past methanotrophs.
Diffusion is slow through peat full of undecayed organic matter, and matters more in drier, loosely packed soils, since methane moves faster through soil than water.
Aerenchyma, porous tissue in some plants, lets methane shunt straight from the roots to the air, bypassing oxidation.
In ebullition, methane builds up in soil pockets until the pressure bursts, releasing it too fast for methanotrophs to consume it; piezometers detect these pockets.

title: Controls on wetland methane flux
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Controlling factors

definition.text: The factors, chiefly water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production, that set how much wetland methane reaches the atmosphere.

facts.text: Net flux depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens reaches the surface before methanotrophs oxidize it.
Large methane fluxes have followed drought-driven drops in the water table; with water at or above the surface, ebullition and plant transport dominate.
Soil temperature sets microbial production and consumption rates, and with the water table drives seasonal cycles.
Soils rich in acetate or hydrogen and CO2 favour methane production; steady cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 are optimal.

title: Wetland nitrous oxide fluxes
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Nitrous oxide fluxes

definition.text: The exchange of nitrous oxide between wetland soils and the air, which can run in either direction.

facts.text: Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential 300 times that of CO2 and is the leading ozone-depleting emission of the 21st century.
Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, raise wetland soil N2O fluxes through denitrification and nitrification.
Measured fluxes range from 0.14 to 23.83 μmol N2O m−2 h−1 in mangroves of Shenzhen and Hong Kong, and negative fluxes, caused by soil consumption, are common.

title: Wetland drainage and methane
article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Human development of wetlands

definition.text: The mixed effect on methane emissions of draining wetlands for development, housing and farming.

facts.text: Lowering the water table increases methane consumption by soil methanotrophs and can turn a wetland from a methane source into a sink.
Drainage ditches that stay saturated, especially when drains are too close together, become warm wet mini-wetlands that emit much methane.

title: Land use, land-use change, and forestry
article: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: The greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals that result from human land use, land-use change and forestry.

facts.text: LULUCF activities can add carbon dioxide to or remove it from the atmosphere through their effects on the carbon cycle, but are difficult to measure.
The IPCC estimates land-use change, such as turning forest into farmland, adds a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt of carbon a year, against 6.3 ± 0.6 Gt from fossil fuels and cement.
Updated assessments put LULUCF emissions at 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt C (4.1 ± 2.6 Gt CO2) a year over 2014–2023.
Under Kyoto, accounting is mandatory for afforestation, reforestation and deforestation, and voluntary for forest, cropland and grazing land management.
Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration; a 2021 study found it affected 17% of land in 1960–2019.

sources.title: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: The release of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, to the atmosphere from human activities and natural sources such as wetlands.

facts.text: Rising methane emissions cause up to one-third of near-term global heating; in 2019 about 60% came from human activities and 40% from natural sources.
Most natural emissions come from methanogens producing methane in warm, moist soils and in animal guts.
Wetlands supply about three-quarters of the enduring natural sources of methane.
Plant agriculture contributes about 15% of human emissions, with rice the largest single source: waterlogged paddies act like wetlands, emitting about 30 of 400 million tonnes in 2022.
Converting forests to farmland adds soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation, and changing the water table shifts a soil between methane source and sink.

definition.text: Bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of carbon and energy.

facts.text: They live in wetlands, soils, marshes, rice paddies and landfills, mostly near methane sources, though some oxidize atmospheric methane.
By cutting the methane that reaches the atmosphere, they play a significant role in the global methane budget.
Aerobic methanotrophs combine oxygen and methane to form formaldehyde, built into organic compounds, and carbon dioxide; the first step uses methane monooxygenase enzymes.
Type I methanotrophs tend to dominate cold, oxygen-poor, methane-rich settings; Type II are more stress-tolerant and dominate methane-limited and acidic ones.
In anoxic soils, rice paddies and sediments, some methanotrophs oxidize methane using nitrate, nitrite, iron, sulfate or manganese instead of oxygen.

definition.text: Returning a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate again.

facts.text: It keeps the soil moist and slows drainage by blocking and filling canals and digging deep wells.
Peat dams are built from stable, impermeable, erosion-resistant unoxidized peat dug from the channel bottom.
Plastic dams of interlocking piling can hold deep pools but work only on peat, not on mineral soil.

definition.text: Rewetting drained peatlands while continuing to farm them with crops suited to wet conditions.

facts.text: Raising the water table restores the peatland ecosystem that stores large amounts of carbon, so the land serves as both carbon sink and farmland.
Possible crops include berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel.
Degraded farmed peatlands are often nutrient-rich; paludiculture can remove the excess nutrients over time, a cheaper alternative to stripping the topsoil.

definition.text: The consumption of methane, including atmospheric methane, by methanotrophic microbes in soils, which makes soils a natural methane sink.

facts.text: Converting forests and natural land to farmland raises soil nitrogen, which inhibits methane oxidation by methanotrophs.
Changing the water table directly shifts a soil between acting as a methane source or sink.
Lowering a wetland's water table increases soil methanotroph consumption and can turn it into a methane sink.
Nutrient-supplemented landfill cover soils can act as small methane sinks as abundant methanotrophs consume methane.

title: Earth system and land surface models

definition.text: Computer models that represent the land surface, including vegetation, soil and terrain, within simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles.

facts.text: A land surface model combining vegetation cover, soil type and terrain with rainfall data estimates how much water soaks into the ground and how much becomes streamflow.
Earth system models extend climate models to include the biosphere and land use change.
They predict a wide range of future land and ocean carbon uptake even under identical emission scenarios.
Peatlands are still omitted from the main Earth system models, although their carbon balance is expected to shift from sink to source this century.
